content: In the United States, a Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA), Patient Care Assistant (PCA), State Tested Nurse Aid (STNA), or Nursing Assistant-Registered (NA/R) is an individual who provides assistance to patients, clients, or service users with healthcare needs. This includes helping with activities of daily living (ADLs) and delivering bedside care, which often involves basic nursing procedures. These tasks are performed under the supervision of a Registered Nurse (RN) or a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN). In the United Kingdom and other countries, similar roles may be referred to as Nursing Assistant (NA), Auxiliary Nurse (Aux-N), Patient Care Associate (PCA), Nursing Tech (NT), Healthcare Assistant (HCA), Healthcare Support Worker (HSW), or Clinical Support Worker (CSW). Despite the variation in titles, the responsibilities and scope of the role remain consistent. Nursing Assistants are integral members of the healthcare team. They often possess significant experience and skill but may be restricted from performing certain tasks due to legal and liability concerns. Efforts to regulate and standardize their education and qualifications have led to the establishment of credentials like the North American CNA. This certification is obtained by completing the required workplace experience and academic training, which is then registered with a central body. Such certification allows employers to verify the individual’s qualifications and helps prevent those who have had their certification revoked from continuing to work in healthcare roles. In the UK, the credibility of Healthcare Assistants and other social care workers has been bolstered by mandatory registration with the General Social Care Council in England (or equivalent bodies in Scotland and Wales) since 2009. In modern hospitals and extended care facilities, Nursing Assistants play a crucial role in the healthcare team, which includes various personnel beyond nurses. They provide routine care, enabling nurses to focus on tasks that only they are authorized to perform, such as formulating care plans, conducting nursing assessments, administering medications, and assisting in surgical preparation. These responsibilities are defined by each state’s Nurse Practice Acts. Nursing Assistants must not only be proficient in performing procedures but also be skilled in observing patients’ conditions and reporting their findings to the nurse. Since nurses often cannot spend extended periods in the patient’s room, Nursing Assistants are frequently referred to as the nurse’s eyes and ears. Nursing Assistants are typically responsible for assisting with Activities of Daily Living, such as bathing and feeding patients. They must also be well-versed in emergency procedures, remain calm under pressure, and be capable of initiating a code blue and performing CPR effectively. In March 2007, the National Center for Health Statistics published a 62-page document titled An Introduction to the National Nursing Assistant Survey, which provides insights into the role and responsibilities of Nursing Assistants. Federal regulations for nurse aide training in the United States were established under the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1987 (OBRA 1987). State-approved training programs must include a minimum of 75 hours of instruction, with at least 16 hours of supervised clinical training. Individuals who complete these programs are recognized as Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs) or State Tested Nurse Aides (STNAs) and are listed on the state registry of nursing aides. To maintain certification, all nurse aides must complete 12 hours of continuing education annually. To become a state-certified Nursing Assistant, individuals must master a set of basic skills required to care for patients in both long-term care facilities and home settings. While these skills are primarily geared toward the care of elderly patients, they are applicable to a wide range of nursing assistant roles. Nursing Assistants are commonly employed in hospital units, although some units, particularly high-stress areas like Critical Care Units (CCU) or Intensive Care Units (ICU), may not utilize Nursing Assistants due to the critical condition of the patients.
